mcqs.question: The sliding-window solution for the longest substring without repeating characters uses two indices and a Set. What is its time complexity, and why?
options: O(n): each unit is inserted into the Set at most once and removed at most once, so the total work of both loops together is bounded by a constant per unit.
O(n²): a while loop is nested inside the for loop, so the worst case is n times n iterations.
O(n log n): Set operations cost log n on average and there are n of them.
O(min(n, distinct units)): the running time matches the Set's size bound.
mcqs.explanation: Correct because the left index never moves backwards: every shrink of the window consumes work that was prepaid by an earlier insertion, so each unit is added and removed at most once and the nested shape still amortizes to O(n). The strongest distractor is option 1: multiplying loop counts is only valid when the inner loop can restart from scratch on every outer iteration, which the monotonic left pointer makes impossible. Option 3 quotes the space bound, O(min(n, distinct-unit-count)), not the time bound.

mcqs.question: For a search box that may receive multi-code-point emoji, what does Array.from(text) give the longest-unique-substring algorithm, and what does it still not give?
options: Unicode code points, one per element; it does not segment grapheme clusters, so one user-perceived character can occupy several elements.
UTF-16 code units, exactly like direct string indexing, so surrogate pairs are split into two elements.
Grapheme clusters, one per user-perceived character, because Array.from splits text on perceived boundaries.
The same count as text.length: both count UTF-16 code units, so the choice cannot change the result.
mcqs.explanation: Correct: Array.from iterates code points, the safe default over raw indexing, but an emoji with a skin-tone modifier or a ZWJ sequence is several code points, so grapheme-level uniqueness needs a separate segmentation step and must be clarified as a requirement. The strongest distractor is option 2, which overcredits Array.from: it stops at code points and knows nothing about user-perceived boundaries. Option 1 describes direct string indexing, and option 3 wrongly assumes text.length counts what Array.from yields.

mcqs.question: Records arrive from several paginated responses, each parsed separately, so the same record can appear as two distinct objects. Which implementation dedupes by id, keeps the first-seen record and its position, and runs in O(n) average time?
options: return [...new Set(records)]: Set stores unique values and iterates in insertion order.
Filter with a Set of ids: skip a record whose id is already present, otherwise add the id and keep the record.
Sort the records by id, then remove adjacent duplicates.
Filter with a nested scan: keep a record only if no previously kept record has the same id.
mcqs.explanation: Correct: an explicit stable key (id) with Set membership gives O(n) average time and preserves first-seen order, which is exactly the bank's pattern. The strongest distractor is option 0: everything stated about Set is true (unique values, insertion order), but membership uses identity-based equality, so two separately created object literals with identical fields are both kept and nothing is deduped. Option 2 breaks the first-seen-position requirement and costs O(n log n); option 3 produces correct output but degrades to O(n²) on large merges.

mcqs.question: A breadth-first walk over a large menu uses a plain array plus a `head` index (`const node = queue[head++]`) instead of `queue.shift()`. Which cost argument actually justifies that choice?
options: `shift()` removes from the tail, so a FIFO queue built on it would silently become LIFO and the walk would turn depth-first.
`shift()` is O(1) amortized in every modern engine, so the head index only saves a method call and the gain is constant-factor noise.
`shift()` moves every remaining element down one index, so n dequeues copy about n²/2 elements; the head index dequeues with a read and never reindexes.
`shift()` can hand the same node out twice when the array is appended to during the walk, so a head index is required for correctness.
mcqs.explanation: Correct: the language gives no O(1) dequeue. `Array.prototype.shift` removes index 0 and then moves every remaining element down one slot (ECMAScript, https://tc39.es/ecma262/#sec-array.prototype.shift), so draining a queue of n nodes performs about n²/2 element moves, while a monotonic `head` index turns each dequeue into one indexed read and keeps the whole traversal at O(v + e). The strongest distractor is option 1, the belief that engines hide the cost: draining 10k, 20k and 40k entries in Node took 1.6 ms, 21.9 ms and 83.8 ms — roughly 4× per doubling, which is the quadratic curve, not constant-factor noise; even where an engine special-cases an array shape, the language guarantees nothing, so the queue has to be reasoned about portably. Option 0 confuses the end of the array with the end of the queue: `shift()` removes the first element, which is exactly the FIFO end. Option 3 names a real hazard — mutating a collection while iterating it — but not this one: the array is only appended to with children and read through the advancing index, so no node is dequeued twice.

mcqs.question: Which statement about memoizing an expensive derived value for a filterable list is correct?
options: Memoization makes the first computation cheaper by caching partial results during the initial run.
A Map keyed by the argument's identity stays correct even if callers mutate the argument between calls, because Map re-hashes the contents on lookup.
Memoization avoids repeating work for inputs already seen; it does not make the first computation cheaper and does not replace rendering only the rows that are needed.
An unbounded cache is safe for free-text query keys because Map evicts stale entries with LRU behavior.
mcqs.explanation: Correct, and it is the bank's exact caution: a cache only pays off on repeated inputs, so cold queries are as slow as before, and caching a derived array does nothing about rendering thousands of DOM rows. The strongest distractor is option 1: Map keys use identity-based equality, so a mutated-but-same-reference argument is a cache hit that returns stale data; the key must represent every input affecting the result, via immutable inputs or explicit versioning. Option 3 invents eviction: Map has none, which is why unbounded keys must be bounded by design.

mcqs.question: Two handlers, two goals: (1) a search input where only the settled query should reach the API; (2) a scroll listener that must repaint a sticky badge while the user keeps scrolling. Which pairing of debounce and throttle is right, and why?
options: Throttle the search, debounce the scroll: rate-limit the typing evenly, and let the badge settle once the gesture ends instead of repainting mid-scroll.
Debounce the search, throttle the scroll: one request after typing stops, and at most one repaint per interval while scroll events keep arriving.
Debounce both: debounce is the stricter schedule, so it also covers a stream that never pauses, which a throttle cannot.
Use requestAnimationFrame for both: it runs the callback at most once per frame, so it replaces debounce or throttle with a better interval.
mcqs.explanation: Correct, because the two schedules answer different questions: debounce restarts its timer on every call and fires once after `wait` ms of silence, which is exactly "only the settled query"; throttle fires at most once per interval while calls continue, which is exactly "repaint regularly during the gesture" (web.dev, https://web.dev/articles/debounce-your-input-handlers). The strongest distractor is option 2: it sounds like a superset, but a debounce whose timer restarts on every event fires *never* while the stream is continuous — measured with 30 ms scroll events for 300 ms, a 100 ms debounce fired zero times during the burst and once after it — so it is a different firing schedule, not a stricter version of throttle, and it guarantees nothing about a scroll that lasts 30 seconds. Option 0 inverts both requirements: a throttled search sends interim queries mid-word, and a debounced scroll freezes the badge for the whole gesture. Option 3 miscasts rAF: it fires once per frame with no configurable interval, so it rate-limits nothing on the server side; for scroll work it is the right frame-alignment tool on top of a light handler, which complements throttle rather than replacing it.

mcqs.question: Which group contains only values that `structuredClone()` preserves and a `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify())` round trip does not?
options: A `Map` with entries, a `Date`, and an object that references itself: the clone keeps all three, JSON loses or rejects each.
A function, a live DOM node, and a `Promise`: the clone copies all three, while JSON drops or flattens them.
A `Set` of ids, a `WeakMap` and a cycle: the clone survives all three, while JSON collapses the first two and throws on the cycle.
None of them: both are deep copies of the same value graph and differ only in speed and memory use.
mcqs.explanation: Correct: `structuredClone` runs the structured-clone algorithm the platform uses for `postMessage` and IndexedDB, so a `Map` or `Set` comes back with its entries, a `Date` with its instant, and a cycle pointing into the copy; the JSON round trip is a serializer, so `Map`/`Set` stringify to `{}`, a `Date` returns as an ISO string, and a cycle throws `TypeError` (MDN, https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Window/structuredClone). The strongest distractor is option 2, because its JSON half is exactly right — `JSON.stringify(new Set([1, 2]))` is `{}` and a cycle throws `TypeError: Converting circular structure to JSON` — while its clone half is false: `WeakMap` has no cloneable representation, and `structuredClone(new WeakMap())` throws `DataCloneError`. Option 1 is the same overreach from the other side, "it is a deep clone, so it copies anything", when functions, `Promise`s and most DOM nodes are precisely what it throws on; option 3 ignores that the two paths agree only on the plain-JSON subset of the graph.

mcqs.question: A route runs three independent fetches under Promise.all and one rejects. What happens to the other two network requests?
options: They are cancelled automatically: Promise.all's rejection propagates to sibling promises.
They keep running to completion; the rejection only abandons waiting for them, and cancelling them requires an AbortSignal passed to each fetch.
They are paused until the rejection is handled, then resumed or cancelled by the handler.
They resolve normally but Promise.all discards their results, which amounts to the same thing as cancelling them.
mcqs.explanation: Correct: Promise.all preserves input order and rejects on the first rejection, but rejection does not cancel the remaining operations; without signals the siblings still consume bandwidth and resolve into nothing. The strongest distractor is option 3: it is half right (their results are indeed discarded) and draws the wrong conclusion, since the requests still complete and the wasted work is observable on the network. Option 0 is the classic conflation of fail-fast observation with cancellation, the exact mix-up of concurrency, cancellation, and stale-result protection the bank warns about.

mcqs.question: What is the output order of: console.log('task start'); queueMicrotask(() => console.log('microtask')); setTimeout(() => console.log('timer task'), 0); console.log('task end');?
options: task start, microtask, task end, timer task
task start, task end, timer task, microtask
task start, task end, microtask, timer task
task start, timer task, task end, microtask
mcqs.explanation: Correct: the two synchronous logs run first; after the current task finishes the browser drains the microtask queue before returning to the event loop, so the microtask runs before the zero-delay timer task, exactly the bank's example. The strongest distractor is option 0: it assumes queueMicrotask runs its callback inline at the enqueue point, which would make microtasks indistinguishable from synchronous code. Option 1 reverses the drain rule by letting a task (the timer) run before pending microtasks, and option 2 treats setTimeout(..., 0) as synchronous.

mcqs.question: In a TreeWalker, an element matches the private-subtree rule. What is the difference between returning FILTER_REJECT and FILTER_SKIP for that element?
options: REJECT excludes the element and its entire subtree; SKIP excludes only the element and still visits its children.
REJECT aborts the whole traversal with an error; SKIP is the safe non-throwing variant.
They are equivalent for elements; the constants only differ for text and comment nodes.
SKIP excludes the element's subtree while REJECT excludes only the element itself.
mcqs.explanation: Correct: the bank's walker returns FILTER_REJECT for a private element precisely so its descendants are excluded, while non-target elements get FILTER_SKIP so traversal still descends into them. The strongest distractor is option 3, which inverts the semantics and would leak private text exactly like the naive simplification. Option 2 is plausible because the two constants do behave the same for NodeIterator (children are still visited), but for TreeWalker the subtree pruning is the entire point of REJECT.

mcqs.question: `flattenIterative` pushes `node.slice().reverse()` onto a stack whose elements are removed with `pop()`. What does the `reverse()` do for correctness, and what breaks if it is dropped?
options: It protects the input: `reverse()` mutates in place, so the children must be copied before they are pushed.
It makes the leftmost child pop first: the stack is LIFO, so reversing before pushing preserves left-to-right output order; without it, siblings come out reversed at every level.
It switches the traversal from depth-first to breadth-first, which a flatten needs for stable output order.
It stops `pop()` from handing out a live reference into the input, which would make the output share nested arrays with the argument.
mcqs.explanation: Correct: the stack inverts order on its own, so pushing a parent's children backwards is what restores the original order when they are popped. `flattenIterative([1, [2, 3]])` yields `[1, 2, 3]` only because of that reverse; keep the `slice()` and drop the `reverse()` and the output is still fully flattened, but `[3, 2, 1]` — the reshape is right, the order contract is broken. The strongest distractor is option 0: `reverse()` really does mutate in place, which is exactly why `slice()` is there, but the copy serves the input's safety while the reverse serves the output's order — two different jobs that the option fuses. Option 2 is a category error: an explicit stack reproduces depth-first order, and flatten is an order contract, not a scheduling strategy. Option 3 invents a sharing hazard that does not exist here: flatten emits leaf values and reuses object references by design, so it is a reshape, not a clone.

mcqs.question: The retry helper waits `Math.random() * Math.min(capMs, baseMs * 2 ** attempt)`. Which statement states the purpose of that sampling correctly, including what it does not achieve?
options: It guarantees that two clients never retry in the same millisecond, because a uniform sample makes a collision impossible.
It keeps the expected wait the same for every attempt, so the server sees a flat retry rate instead of a rising one.

It decorrelates clients that failed together by spreading each retry across the whole `[0, cap]` window, so retries stop arriving in synchronized waves; it does not change the attempt count or raise the cap.
It removes the need for `capMs`, since randomness bounds the delay statistically even while the exponent keeps growing.
mcqs.explanation: Correct: capped backoff alone still synchronizes a cohort — every client that failed at the same instant computes the same delay and hits the server together, one wave per attempt. Sampling uniformly from zero through the cap scatters that cohort across the window, so load is spread instead of stacked, while the attempt budget and the cap stay as they were. The strongest distractor is option 0: it is one inference away from the truth, but the support includes values arbitrarily close to zero, so near-simultaneous retries remain possible — the mechanism lowers collision probability, it does not remove collisions. Option 1 inverts the effect: the expected wait is `cap / 2`, which grows with every attempt and then sits at the cap. Option 3 deletes the only structural bound: a sample proportional to an unbounded exponential grows with it, which is the failure the cap exists to prevent.

mcqs.question: Run the bank's `deepEqual` skeleton on two distinct Dates: it checks `Object.is(a, b)`, then prototypes, then compares `Reflect.ownKeys`. What does `deepEqual(new Date(0), new Date(999))` return, and why?
options: `true`: both have the same prototype and no own keys, so the two instants are never compared.
`false`: `Object.is` compares the contents of `Date` objects, and these two instants differ.
`false`: each `Date` instance has its own prototype object, so the prototype check rejects the pair.
It throws a `TypeError`, because `Reflect.ownKeys` is only defined for plain objects.
mcqs.explanation: Correct, and it is the concrete proof that deep equality is a contract rather than a universal rule: a `Date` keeps its instant in an internal slot, not in an own property, so a key-driven comparison sees two empty shells and declares them equal — the same blind spot makes `new Map([['a', 1]])` equal to `new Map()`. The strongest distractor is option 1: `Object.is` is SameValue, and for objects SameValue is reference identity (with the `NaN` and signed-zero special cases), so it never looks inside an object; two distinct Dates simply fail that step and fall through to the key comparison, which is where the information is lost. Option 2 contradicts how prototypes work — both instances share `Date.prototype` — and option 3 is false: `Reflect.ownKeys` accepts any object, Dates and Maps included, and returns an empty list for both.

mcqs.question: In `enrich`, `userById` is built once and then queried with `userById.get(order.userId)` inside `orders.map`. A reviewer claims the function is still O(n·m). Which reading is correct?
options: O(n·m): the lookup runs inside the `map` callback, so it is an inner loop like any other.
O(n + m log m): building the `Map` sorts the keys, and the insertions pay for that ordering.
O(n log m): `Map` keeps its keys ordered and `get` binary-searches them.
O(n + m) on average: one insertion per user plus one average-constant probe per order, because the index is built once outside the loop.
mcqs.explanation: Correct: one pass builds the index (`m` insertions) and one pass walks the orders (`n` probes), and each probe is average constant time, so the nested shape collapses into a join. The strongest distractor is option 0, because it applies the right reflex — a call inside a loop is an inner loop — to the wrong structure: what decides the cost is how much work repeats per item, and here the repeated work is a single probe into a structure that was built once; move the `new Map(...)` inside the callback and the reviewer's bound becomes correct, which is precisely why hoisting it is the whole optimization. Options 1 and 2 invent ordering that `Map` does not have: iteration follows insertion order, and lookups are average-constant hash probes, not a sorted search. The `average` qualifier is not decoration: with keys that are objects compared by identity, or two records sharing an id, the join does not get slower — it returns a wrong answer, which is why the key must be a stable primitive.

scenarios.prompt: A dashboard route runs loadDashboard() on entry, may unmount before the fetches finish, and can be re-entered quickly. (1) Name every correctness and efficiency problem in this code. (2) Rewrite it so the three resources load concurrently, obsolete results can never render, and navigation cancels work. (3) State what changes if partial data is useful.
rubric: Identifies the waterfall: independent operations awaited one by one instead of started together, so latency sums.
Uses Promise.all for all-or-nothing loading and can state its exact semantics: preserves input order, rejects on first rejection, does not cancel the remaining operations.
Adds cancellation: one AbortSignal passed to every fetch, abort() on route change and cleanup, AbortError treated as expected rather than an error.
Guards rendering with request identity (current controller or version), so a slower obsolete load cannot overwrite newer data even while the component is still mounted.
Knows the partial-data alternative: Promise.allSettled with per-outcome rendering, and checks response.ok before parsing.

scenarios.prompt: This utility ships in a widget bundle. QA reports two symptoms: every search request goes out with the query `undefined`, and the badge does not move until the user stops scrolling. (1) List the defects in `debounce` and in its two uses, and tie each symptom to its cause. (2) Write a production version and spell out its API contract. (3) Explain what the scroll badge needs instead, what teardown must do, and which failure debounce cannot fix even when it is implemented correctly.
rubric: Names the dropped arguments and `this` as the cause of the `undefined` query, and fixes it by forwarding the latest arguments in the trailing call.
Requires `cancel()` plus `removeEventListener` on named handlers at teardown, so no trailing call and no in-flight reply can render for a destroyed widget.
Separates rate from order: shows that a correct debounce still lets a slow earlier response repaint over a newer one, and threads an abort (or request id) through the search.
Diagnoses the badge as a firing-schedule problem — a trailing debounce fires zero times during a continuous gesture — and replaces it with a light passive handler plus an rAF-batched write.
States the API contract (edge, `maxWait` decision, measured delay) instead of shipping trailing-only by default, and keeps rate limiting distinct from frame alignment.

scenarios.prompt: mergePages combines users from several paginated API responses; the same user can appear on more than one page, and each page is parsed separately, so duplicates are distinct objects. (1) Explain precisely why the current implementation removes nothing. (2) Rewrite it so the last-seen record wins while every id stays at the position where it was first seen. (3) State the complexity and what you would ask the product owner first.
rubric: Explains the identity-versus-structural failure precisely: Set keeps both separately parsed objects because object values compare by reference, not by structure.
Keys by the stable id and states the conflict rule (last-wins here) before or while coding.
Knows Map re-set semantics: the value is replaced while the key keeps its first-insertion position, yielding last-wins values in first-seen order.
States O(n) average time and O(n) additional space, and avoids sort-then-dedupe, which breaks first-seen order and costs O(n log n).

scenarios.prompt: The team uses this to prefetch a list of pages with limit 3. A caller asserts that results arrive in input order and the assertion fails intermittently. (1) Explain the order bug and why it is intermittent. (2) The utility also silently misbehaves for some limit values and has an unstated failure contract; identify both. (3) Fix the code and write down the guarantees the fixed version gives.
rubric: Diagnoses the order bug: push-in-completion-order versus assignment at the original index, and explains the intermittency (it depends on task timing).
Preserves the at-most-limit invariant with the worker-pool pull loop rather than starting all tasks at once.
Validates the limit as a positive integer instead of silently returning wrong output for 0, negatives, or fractions.
States the failure contract: fail-fast rejection leaves in-flight tasks running (observed, not cancelled), or offers per-item outcomes or AbortSignal-based cancellation.
Notes what the limit does and does not promise: caps simultaneous resource use; no throughput guarantee, no faster individual tasks.

scenarios.prompt: A payments widget calls `retry(sendOrder)` and ships with this helper. (1) With `retries = 3`, `baseMs = 200` and `capMs = 5000`, how many times can `task` be called, and which delay is awaited before the helper gives up anyway? (2) List the defects and what each one costs the caller. (3) Rewrite it so exhaustion rejects with the last error, the wait is abortable, and the jitter actually desynchronizes clients. (4) Explain why `+ Math.random() * 100` is not jitter in the sense that matters, and name what the caller still has to decide.
rubric: Counts the four invocations correctly and identifies the 1600 ms (plus noise) wait that precedes an unavoidable failure — the bug is in the wait, not in the attempt budget.
Rejects with the original error, preserving status/identity, instead of a generic message.
Makes the backoff wait abortable: clears the timer and rejects with the abort reason so cancellation is immediate rather than one backoff late.
Uses jitter proportional to the capped delay (`random(0, cap)`) and explains decorrelation, not fixed additive noise.
Keeps retry classification and idempotency at the caller, and names the missing total deadline as a separate limit.

scenarios.prompt: This `deepEqual` backs a memoized panel in a selector and compares normalized store snapshots. (1) Give one concrete input per defect and say whether the error is a false positive or a false negative. (2) Name an input on which it does not terminate, and what the runtime does. (3) Rewrite it with an explicit contract, and state the limitation your cycle handling introduces. (4) Say why it should not be the selector's default comparison.
rubric: Gives a concrete input per defect and labels the direction (NaN as a false negative, `[]` versus `{}` as a false positive), rather than listing categories.
Explains `===` versus `Object.is`, including the signed-zero decision as a documented contract choice.
Adds the prototype check before keys and compares own enumerable keys on both sides — filtering `Reflect.ownKeys` so an array's non-enumerable `length` does not reject equal arrays.
Makes cycles terminate with pair tracking and describes it as a bisimulation-style contract line, not just 'add a visited Set'.
Rejects deep equality in the selector: names a cheaper signal (identity, version, normalized fields) and notes the Map/Set cost consequence.
